The world of the Gospels

Jewish and Roman finds that set the scene for the Gospels. These are not Christian artifacts.

Caiaphas family ossuary

everyday object / burial (Jewish context)

1st century AD (ossuary use); tomb found 1990

A limestone bone box inscribed with a name matching the high-priestly family in the Gospels. It belongs to Jewish burial practice of the Second Temple period.

Found: Peace Forest, Jerusalem · Now: Israel Museum, Jerusalem

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Jerusalem ossuary of the period bears the name Joseph son of Caiaphas.

Scholars infer: Likely the high priest Joseph Caiaphas known from Josephus and the New Testament.

Still debated: Whether this exact box held the high priest himself (vs. a relative of the same name).

Commons ↗

Pilate Stone (Caesarea inscription)

inscription (Jewish/Roman context)

AD 26–36 (Pilate’s prefecture); stone found 1961

A Latin building dedication naming “[Pon]tius Pilatus, Prefect of Judea.” It is independent Roman evidence for the prefect named in the Gospels.

Found: Caesarea Maritima, Israel · Now: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (copy often displayed at Caesarea)

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Roman official named Pontius Pilatus held the title prefect of Judea and dedicated a Tiberieum at Caesarea.

Scholars infer: Usual reconstruction of the damaged lines; that this is the same Pilate as in the passion narratives.

Still debated: Exact wording of some restored letters; the stone is not a Christian artifact.

Commons ↗ Britannica ↗

Pool of Siloam

site (Jewish / Gospel-world context)

Second Temple period pool; stepped pool excavated 2004 onward

A large stepped pool fed by the Gihon spring via Hezekiah’s Tunnel. John’s Gospel places a healing of a blind man here.

Found: City of David / Silwan, Jerusalem · Now: In situ (archaeological park area)

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A monumental Second Temple–period pool exists at the traditional Siloam location.

Scholars infer: This is the pool known to first-century Jerusalem and to the Johannine narrative setting.

Still debated: Full extent and phases of the complex; how visitors should picture the Gospel scene.

AD 30–70 · Earliest years

Guiding questions
  • What happened after Jesus' death?
  • How did the apostles organize communities?
  • Where, how often, and how did Christians gather and worship?
  • How does the Eucharist relate historically to the Last Supper?
  • What did Peter, James, John, Paul and others do?
  • What happened as the apostles died?

Surviving narrative and letters for this generation are almost entirely canonical New Testament texts. External notices are brief and later copied. Silence is not evidence.

Meanwhile in the world
after 30 BCE

Egypt: decades after Cleopatra’s death (30 BCE), Egypt is a Roman province — the movie Cleopatra era is already over.

source
41–54

Rome: Claudius is emperor; Rome invades Britain in 43 (the start of Roman Britain).

source
25–220

China: Eastern (Later) Han dynasty rules from Luoyang — a global anchor far from the Mediterranean.

source
54–68

Rome: Nero is emperor — the villain of countless movies and novels about Rome.

source
60 or 61

Britain: Boudica (Boudicca) leads the Iceni revolt against Rome — Warrior Queen territory.

source
64 legend

Rome: Great Fire of Rome under Nero (the “fiddled while Rome burned” story is later legend).

source
66–70

Judaea: First Jewish Revolt; Titus takes Jerusalem and destroys the Second Temple in 70.

source
c. 1–100

Mexico: Teotihuacán growing into a major city — pyramids rising while Nero rules Rome.

source

Evidence shows: New Testament texts that Christians preserved as scripture describe early Jerusalem and diaspora communities, a shared meal tradition, and named leaders; Josephus mentions James; Roman historians mention Christians in connection with Rome under Nero and Claudius.

Historians infer: Frequency of gatherings, exact local variety of meal practice, and day-to-day organization beyond what the texts happen to mention.

Still unknown: The full sequence of events after many apostles' deaths; most local community records; nearly all liturgical detail outside a few New Testament passages.

Discovery

Things people made or used in this period.

Capernaum “House of Peter”

house church / memorial site

1st-century house remains; Christian meeting use by ~late 1st–4th c.; octagonal memorial church later

ⓘ Read with care

Tradition links this house to Peter; archaeology shows a house later treated as sacred, but the identification with Peter himself is debated.

Excavators found a first-century house whose main room was later plastered, inscribed, and set apart, then covered by an octagonal church. Pilgrims remembered it as Peter’s home.

Found: Capernaum (Kfar Nahum), Sea of Galilee, Israel · Now: Under the modern memorial church; Franciscan Custody / IAA oversight of excavations

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Capernaum house was adapted for Christian gathering and later monumentalized.

Scholars infer: Early local memory linked the house to Peter and to Jesus’ Capernaum ministry.

Still debated: Whether the house actually belonged to Peter; how early the Christian use began.

AD 70–150 · After the apostles

Guiding questions
  • How was apostolic teaching transmitted?
  • Who led afterward?
  • What about bishops, presbyters, and deacons?
  • What did ordinary Christian life, prayer, baptism, and Sunday worship look like?
  • How did churches communicate and stay united?
  • What did Christians believe before the later councils?

This is the densest surviving Christian letter-and-manual layer after the New Testament. Many texts traditionally linked to the apostles belong here.

Meanwhile in the world

✦ Fun overlaps

Pompeii dies, Colosseum opens — within a year

Vesuvius buries Pompeii in 79; Titus inaugurates the Colosseum with games in 80 — both just after the apostles’ generation.

source

Cai Lun’s paper and Ignatius/Trajan

Around Ignatius’s letters (c. 107–110) and Pliny–Trajan (c. 112), Cai Lun was at the Eastern Han court; he reported improved papermaking c. 105.

source · source

70

Judaea: Titus takes Jerusalem; Second Temple destroyed.

source

Italy: Mount Vesuvius erupts — Pompeii and Herculaneum buried (the disaster in every volcano documentary).

source
80

Rome: Colosseum inaugurated with games — gladiators for real, not just in movies.

source
98–117

Rome: Trajan emperor; the empire reaches its widest eastern extent.

source
c. 105

China: Cai Lun reports improved papermaking to the Eastern Han court.

source
117–138

Rome: Hadrian; Hadrian’s Wall begun in Britain (122s) — still walkable today.

source
25–220

China: Eastern Han continues; Luoyang among the world’s largest cities.

source
c. 1–200

Mexico: Teotihuacán rising — pyramids of the Sun and Moon taking shape.

source

Evidence shows: Letters from Rome, Antioch, and Smyrna; a church-order manual (Didache); an early martyr narrative for Polycarp; Pliny's provincial procedure under Trajan.

Historians infer: How universal any one local pattern was; exact authorship of anonymous works.

Still unknown: Most local archives; full biographies of most leaders; whether some manuals describe ideal or actual practice.

Rotas–Sator square (Pompeii)

graffito / word square

Before AD 79 (Pompeii burial under Vesuvius)

ⓘ Read with care

The square is real and early; whether it is Christian at all is still debated.

A five-word Latin palindrome square (ROTAS OPERA TENET AREPO SATOR). Some read a hidden Christian prayer; others see a pagan word-play or magic square.

Found: Pompeii (Palaestra / related finds) · Now: In situ / Pompeii archaeological site documentation; casts and photos widely published

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: The square existed in the Vesuvian cities before 79.

Scholars infer: Possible early Christian presence — or none.

Still debated: Whether the Pompeii squares are Christian at all.

Commons ↗

Rylands Papyrus P52 (John)

manuscript / papyrus

Often placed early–mid 2nd century; some scholars prefer later 2nd / ~200

A tiny scrap of a papyrus codex with John 18 on both sides. It is among the earliest surviving pieces of any New Testament book.

Found: Egypt (acquired early 20th c.; exact find-spot uncertain) · Now: John Rylands Library, University of Manchester

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Greek copy of John’s Gospel circulated in Egypt in a codex format by roughly the 2nd century.

Scholars infer: How early John was composed and how fast it spread; that Christians preferred the codex early.

Still debated: Exact date within the 2nd century (or slightly later).

Seven Letters

Ignatius of Antioch

c. 107–110 Saint / Church Father

Letters traditionally said to have been written on his way to martyrdom in Rome; important for bishop, presbyter, and deacon language. New Advent: middle recension, tr. Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1).

AD 150–325 · Developing Church

Guiding questions
  • How did the Mass and the sacraments take shape?
  • How was doctrine becoming defined?
  • What controversies arose?
  • What effects did persecution have?
  • What was the role of Rome and other churches?
  • How were authoritative writings determined?

From Justin's ritual descriptions through Irenaeus and the African and Latin writers to Eusebius and Nicaea, this period has the richest primary documentation for worship, conflict, and canon.

Meanwhile in the world
161–180

Rome: Marcus Aurelius emperor — the philosopher-emperor; his son Commodus is the villain of the film Gladiator.

source
c. 166

China–Rome contact: a reported envoy from Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus) reaches the Han court.

source
220

China: Han dynasty ends; Three Kingdoms period begins (220–265) — the era of countless East Asian novels and games.

source
224–241

Persia: Ardashīr I founds the Sasanian empire, ending Parthian rule.

source
235–284

Rome: Crisis of the Third Century — emperors rise and fall in rapid succession.

source
c. 200+

Mexico: Teotihuacán a major urban centre (Temple of Quetzalcóatl graves ~200 CE).

source
3rd–4th c.

Africa: Kingdom of Aksum rising as a Red Sea trading power.

source
313

Rome: Edict of Milan — Constantine and Licinius grant toleration for Christianity.

source
325

Nicaea: First Council of Nicaea under Constantine.

source

Evidence shows: Second-century apologies and church manuals; named controversies (Marcion, Gnostic teachers, Quartodeciman Pascha dispute, rebaptism); martyr acts; third-century unity and baptism debates; early fourth-century imperial shift in Lactantius and Eusebius; Nicaea creed and canons.

Historians infer: How typical any one city's liturgy was; motives in polemical sources.

Still unknown: Full texts of many opponents (often known only through critics); exact authorship of some church orders.

Discovery

Things people made or used in this period.

Alexamenos graffito

graffito

Usually late 1st–early 3rd century (often ~AD 200)

A scratched cartoon of a person raising a hand toward a crucified figure with a donkey’s head, with Greek words mocking “Alexamenos” for worshipping his god. One of the earliest pictures of a crucifixion scene.

Found: Palatine Hill, Rome (paedagogium) · Now: Palatine Museum, Rome

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Someone in Rome mocked a person named Alexamenos for worshipping a crucified god.

Scholars infer: The mocked figure is Jesus; the joke reflects pagan contempt for the cross.

Still debated: Exact date; whether the donkey-head is a specific anti-Jewish/anti-Christian slur tradition.

Bodmer papyri (incl. P75 / Hanna Papyrus)

manuscript / papyrus

Roughly late 2nd–early 3rd century for key NT leaves (debated)

Early, carefully written Gospel papyri. P75 is famous for its close kinship to later great parchment Bibles.

Found: Egypt · Now: Bodmer Foundation, Cologny; Vatican Apostolic Library (P75)

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: High-quality Gospel copies existed in Egypt before Constantine’s parchment pandects.

Scholars infer: Pathways from early papyri to Codex Vaticanus-type text.

Still debated: Precise dates; relationship details between P75 and Vaticanus.

Catacomb of Domitilla (arcosolium)

catacomb

2nd–4th centuries (complex grows over time)

Vast underground galleries and painted arcosolia. Domitilla preserves the scale of Christian burial networks under Rome before and after Constantine.

Found: Via Ardeatina, Rome · Now: In situ; open to visitors under Pontifical Commission / site management

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Large organized Christian cemeteries existed beneath Rome.

Scholars infer: Links to Flavian-era Christian households in tradition; growth patterns of the community.

Still debated: Which earliest nuclei are securely Christian vs. mixed.

manuscript / papyrus

A group of early papyrus codices of Scripture — Gospels, Paul, Revelation — showing how third-century Christians copied and carried their books.

Found: Egypt (exact find circumstances partly obscure; acquired 1930s) · Now: Chester Beatty Library, Dublin

Chi-Rho oil lamp (Met)

everyday object

Met: 3rd–7th century (broad)

A small clay lamp stamped with the chi-rho. Someone lit their evening room with Christ’s monogram — faith in the furniture of ordinary life.

Found: Egypt · Now: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (17.194.1813) — Public Domain / CC0 image policy

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

The Met ↗

Christ-Helios mosaic (Tomb of the Julii)

mosaic / tomb

Late 3rd / early 4th century (typical)

A ceiling mosaic of a chariot-riding figure with a rayed nimbus among vines — widely read as Christ using the visual language of Sol Invictus.

Found: Vatican Necropolis (scavi), under St Peter’s Basilica · Now: In situ (scavi); access by Vatican guided tour

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Vatican necropolis tomb mixed Christian and solar imagery before or around Constantine’s time.

Scholars infer: Christ as true “sun” of salvation; deliberate reuse of imperial solar art.

Still debated: Exact date; how consciously “anti-Sol” vs. simply shared artistic vocabulary.

St Peter’s ↗ Commons ↗

Dura-Europos house church & baptistery

house church

Converted ~AD 232–256 (city fell to the Sasanians c. 256)

The earliest securely dated Christian house church. A domestic building was adapted with a meeting hall and a painted baptistery (Good Shepherd, healing scenes, women at the tomb).

Found: Dura-Europos, Syria (block M8) · Now: Wall paintings at Yale University Art Gallery (CC0); site in Syria

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Third-century Christians at Dura baptized in a decorated room and met in a remodeled house.

Scholars infer: How typical this arrangement was; exact reading of some painted scenes.

Still debated: Degree of “church” vs. continuing domestic use; some iconographic identifications.

Yale ↗ Source ↗ Commons ↗

Fractio Panis (breaking of the bread) — Priscilla

catacomb fresco

Often placed 2nd–4th century (Greek Chapel)

A banquet scene with a figure breaking bread at a table — long read as an early image of the Eucharist or agape meal.

Found: Greek Chapel, Catacomb of Priscilla, Rome · Now: In situ; Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Christians painted communal meal imagery in a Roman catacomb chapel.

Scholars infer: Eucharistic meaning (fractio panis); some see a funerary banquet more broadly.

Still debated: How specifically “Mass-like” vs. funerary meal the scene is.

Catacombs ↗ Commons ↗

Good Shepherd fresco (Catacomb of Priscilla)

catacomb fresco

Usually late 2nd–3rd century

Christ as a young shepherd carrying a sheep — tender, everyday imagery in a burial place. Among the best-known early Christian paintings.

Found: Catacomb of Priscilla, Rome · Now: In situ; under Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Roman Christians used shepherd imagery in funerary art well before Constantine.

Scholars infer: Link to John 10 / Luke 15 and to pagan shepherd motifs reused for Christ.

Still debated: Exact chapel date within the catacomb’s long use.

Catacombs ↗ Commons ↗

Good Shepherd — Catacomb of Callixtus (Lucina)

catacomb fresco

3rd century (Crypt of Lucina area)

Another early Good Shepherd in the papal cemetery of Callixtus — the same image language as Priscilla, in the burial ground of many early popes and martyrs.

Found: Catacomb of Callixtus, Rome · Now: In situ; Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Shepherd Christ imagery was shared across major Roman Christian cemeteries.

Scholars infer: Continuity of hope-for-the-dead imagery before public basilicas.

Still debated: Fine-grained dating of individual cubicula.

Catacombs ↗

Inscription of Abercius

inscription

Late 2nd / early 3rd century (Vatican Museums)

A Greek verse epitaph in coded Christian language: a “holy Shepherd,” travel to Rome, “pure fish,” bread and wine. The Vatican calls it the most ancient known Christian inscription.

Found: Hieropolis (Hierapolis area), Phrygia, Turkey — reused in a bath building · Now: Vatican Museums, Museo Pio Cristiano

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A late-2nd/early-3rd-century Phrygian Christian used cryptic Eucharistic and ecclesial imagery on his tomb.

Scholars infer: Abercius was a bishop of Hierapolis; the “queen” is the Roman church.

Still debated: How much of the later Life of Abercius can be trusted beyond the stone.

Vatican ↗ Commons ↗

Livia Primitiva funerary slab (fish & anchor)

inscription / everyday Christian symbol

Usually 3rd century

A simple tomb slab with fish and an anchor — quiet symbols of hope and of Christ the fish (ICHTHYS) that ordinary believers could carve without a long inscription.

Found: Rome (catacomb context; now in museum collections — Louvre often cited for the plaque) · Now: Musée du Louvre, Paris (commonly referenced)

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Fish and anchor were used as Christian funerary signs in Rome.

Back to top

AD 325–1000 · After Constantine

Guiding questions
  • What changed after Constantine?
  • How did buildings, liturgy, vestments, art, and music develop?
  • Which councils clarified teaching?
  • How did monasticism grow?
  • How did East and West diverge?
  • Which early practices survived or changed?

Selective coverage. Favor documents that show practice (Egeria, Cyril's mystagogical lectures, Apostolic Constitutions 8, monastic rules) and the great Christological and creedal councils, plus II Nicaea on images.

Meanwhile in the world

✦ Fun overlaps

Chalcedon and Attila — same year

Council of Chalcedon (451) is the same year a Roman–Visigoth force checked Attila at the Catalaunian Plains.

source · source

Augustine writing while Maya Classic cities rose

Confessions (c. 397–400) and City of God (413–426) overlap the Maya Classic Period (c. 250–900), when Tikal and other cities flourished.

source

Benedict’s Rule and the Arthur legend-setting legend

Benedict’s Rule (c. 530) falls in the post-Roman British centuries where later Arthurian legends are set — Arthur himself is legend, not verified history.

source · source

early 4th–late 6th c.

India: Gupta dynasty — a classical age of literature, math, and art.

source
c. 250–900

Mesoamerica: Maya Classic Period — Tikal, Palenque, Copán (the cities in every Maya documentary).

source
476

West: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus — conventional end of the Western Roman Empire.

source
527–565

Byzantium: Justinian I; Hagia Sophia built.

source
618–907

China: Tang dynasty — often called a golden age of Chinese culture.

source
793

England: Vikings raid Lindisfarne — the attack that opens every Viking Age story.

source
800–814

Europe: Charlemagne crowned emperor of the Romans (800); dies 814.

source
622

Arabia: Hijrah — Muhammad migrates from Mecca to Medina; start of the Muslim era.

source

Evidence shows: Imperial patronage narratives; catechetical and liturgical descriptions; monastic rules; conciliar definitions; pilgrim observation of Jerusalem rites.

Historians infer: How quickly local rites converged; how representative one pilgrim or one rule was.

Still unknown: Continuous musical notation for earliest chant; many ceremonial details before later Ordines.

AD 1000–present · Medieval Church onward

Guiding questions
  • How did the Mass reach recognizable forms?
  • How did spirituality, theology, and devotion develop?
  • Which modern Catholic traditions trace early, and which arose later?

Selective milestones: a short spine of Mass and doctrine documents alongside spiritual classics. These establish official teaching at dated moments; they do not by themselves prove day-to-day parish practice.

Meanwhile in the world

✦ Fun overlaps

1066 still sits on today’s British throne

William wins at Hastings (1066). From his granddaughter Matilda’s son Henry II onward, every English (then British) monarch descends from William — including Charles III.

source · source · source

Teresa of Ávila and Elizabeth I

Teresa’s Life (1565) and Interior Castle (1577) fall squarely in Elizabeth I’s reign (1558–1603) — rival Catholic and Protestant worlds, same decades.

source · source

Shakespeare and Galileo, born the year before Teresa’s Life

Shakespeare baptized 1564; Galileo born 1564 — the year before Teresa’s Life (1565). Both alive through Quo Primum, Interior Castle, and John of the Cross’s 1580s works.

source · source · source

Devout Life while Jamestown and Pocahontas’s world open

Francis de Sales’s Introduction to the Devout Life (1609) lands two years after Jamestown (1607), in the Pocahontas era — and the same years Galileo is turning his telescope on the sky.

source · source

Lateran IV and Magna Carta — same year

Fourth Lateran Council canons and Magna Carta are both dated 1215.

source

Joan of Arc’s lifetime overlaps The Imitation of Christ

Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) is alive across the window usually given for The Imitation of Christ (c. 1418–27).

source

Cahokia a mega-city while Aquinas writes the Summa

Cahokia near today’s St. Louis flourished c. 950–1350 (up to ~20,000 people) — still a major centre when Aquinas wrote the Summa (1265–74) and when Lateran IV met (1215).

source · source

Mansa Musa’s gold hajj before Catherine of Siena

Mansa Musa’s spectacular pilgrimage (1324) is only about fifty years before Catherine’s Dialogue (1377–78).

source · source

Thérèse’s 1890s — baseball already America’s pastime legend

By Story of a Soul (1895–97), baseball was established in the U.S. The Abner Doubleday “invented it in 1839” story is legend, not history.

source · source

Culloden (Outlander) sits between two Deep Dive books

No Deep Dive writing is from 1746, but Culloden — the last Jacobite battle — falls in the long gap between Introduction to the Devout Life (1609) and Story of a Soul (1895–97).

source

c. 950–1350

North America: Cahokia (near today’s St. Louis) flourishes — up to ~20,000 people; largest city north of Mexico before Europeans. (Pre-contact Cherokee politics are mostly unknown from written sources.)

source
1206–27

Asia: Genghis Khan builds the Mongol empire — the conqueror from every world-history classroom.

source
1324

West Africa: Mansa Musa’s gold-laden pilgrimage to Mecca makes Mali famous across the Mediterranean.

source
1412?–31

France: Joan of Arc leads French forces, then is executed (1431) — the Maid of Orléans of stage and screen.

source
c. 1455

Germany: Gutenberg completes his 42-line Bible — movable type that changes Europe.

source
1492 / 1519–21

Atlantic & Mexico: Columbus reaches the Caribbean (1492); Cortés and allies take Tenochtitlán (1521), ending Aztec imperial rule.

source
1509–47

England: Henry VIII reigns — and his six wives become schoolroom legend.

source
1558–1603

England: Elizabeth I; Shakespeare baptized 1564 and Galileo born 1564 — the Tudor/Armada world of film and novels.

source
1607–14 / 1746

Virginia: Jamestown founded 1607; Pocahontas era. Scotland: Culloden 1746 ends the Jacobite rising (Outlander territory) — between Devout Life and Story of a Soul.

source

Evidence shows: Official teaching and rubrical policy at dated moments (councils, papal constitutions, spiritual classics).

Historians infer: Continuity claims with the earliest centuries are historical judgments, not automatic from the texts.

Still unknown: How every parish practiced day to day between these milestones.
